title: How they say it there
job: Regional and generational speech; what marks an outsider
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: 'How they say it there' has a different answer here from any other course on this ladder: Sanskrit has no home vernacular and no regional grammar to teach. What moves across a region is how a word is SAID. evam is 'this way' and anyathā is 'otherwise', and between them they are the whole frame of the module.

deśaḥ is the region and deśe is its 'in' shape, which is the shape every line here writes: mama deśe janāḥ evam vadanti. The observation is always made about a PLACE and never about a person, because no person owns the tradition.
uccāraṇam is the pronunciation and bhedaḥ is the difference. bhedaḥ kevalam uccāraṇe asti — the difference is only in the saying, and the word on the page does not move at all.

The cluster written jñ in IAST, as in jñānam, is the loudest of the three variants: across the north it is said close to 'gy', in Maharashtra close to 'dny', and in the south nearer to the two letters it is spelled with. This course says it the pan-Indian way and spells it one way only.

The vowel written ṛ (U+1E5B) is said with an i-glide across most of the north and east and with a u-glide in parts of the south and west. It costs no new word to hear: kṛṣṇaḥ, vṛddhaḥ, pṛcchati and pṛṣṭhataḥ are already on this ladder and all four carry it.

The visarga (U+1E25) at a pause is a breathy echo of the vowel in front of it, so rāmaḥ ends 'ra-ma-ha'. That one is not regional at all — it is constant, and it is on screen in every module of this course.

English regional difference is a difference of WORDS: lift and elevator, autumn and fall. Sanskrit's is not. The word is the same word everywhere and only its saying moves, so a learner hunting for the local word for something is hunting for a thing that does not exist.

The second axis is register rather than region. śāstram — the recited and the expository — carries full sandhi, long compounds and a slower line; sambhāṣaṇam joins less and keeps its sentences short. sambhāṣaṇam is what this whole course speaks.

saṃskṛtam ekam asti, kintu paramparā ekā na asti. One language, many handed-down traditions of saying it — and the numeral copies the noun's ending every time: ekam beside a neuter, ekā beside a feminine, ekaḥ beside a masculine.

The generational half is a SHAPE and not a list: an older speaker says a word differently and often more slowly, and no list of current words is written here, because such a list dates faster than a course can be maintained. And the honest line about all of it: the tradition this course teaches is a passport and not a disguise. It is understood by teachers and in sambhāṣaṇa classes everywhere, and it makes nobody a local, because there is no local to be.

sentences.display: mama deśe janāḥ evam vadanti, bhavataḥ deśe anyathā vadanti.
sentences.script: मम देशे जनाः एवम् वदन्ति, भवतः देशे अन्यथा वदन्ति।
sentences.cue: In my part of the country people say it this way; in yours they say it differently.
sentences.literal: of-me in-region people thus say, of-you in-region otherwise say

words.note: L1-M1's 'of me'. Here it owns the place rather than the speaking, so mama with the 'in' shape behind it is 'in my region'.
The region, cued for the word and not for the case: deśaḥ names it, deśe is L1-M7's 'in' shape on it, and every line in this module uses the 'in' shape.
L3-M9's janaḥ in its plural. It is people in general here — the speakers of a region, never a named person.
'This way', pointing at a manner and never at a thing. It takes no ending, and it is the first half of the module's frame.
L5-M1's plural of vadati. A region speaks in the plural, so this is the ordinary verb of the module.
L1-M2's 'of you'. With a place noun behind it the genitive owns the noun and the noun keeps its own case: bhavataḥ deśe is 'in your region'.
'Differently', evam's opposite number and the second half of the frame. Like evam it takes no ending — a manner word, which is what L2-M4's katham asks for.

sentences.trap: Nothing in this sentence is about grammar. evam and anyathā are about the SAYING, and the words on either side of the comma are the same words.
sentences.sound: MA-ma DAY-shay JA-naah AY-vam VA-dan-ti, bha-va-TAH DAY-shay an-ya-THAA VA-dan-ti. The visarga of bhavataḥ is an echo of the a in front of it, so on its own it ends 'bha-va-ta-ha'. Said at speed the two joins show: janāḥ evam runs on as janā evam with the visarga dropping before the vowel, and bhavataḥ deśe becomes bhavato deśe before the voiced d.

variations.display: mama deśe janāḥ evam vadanti, bhavatyāḥ deśe anyathā vadanti.
variations.script: मम देशे जनाः एवम् वदन्ति, भवत्याः देशे अन्यथा वदन्ति।
variations.cue: In my part of the country people say it this way; in yours they say it differently.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, so bhavataḥ forks to bhavatyāḥ and nothing else in the line moves

variations.display: kim bhavataḥ deśe janāḥ anyathā vadanti?
variations.script: किम् भवतः देशे जनाः अन्यथा वदन्ति?
variations.cue: Do people say it differently in your part of the country?
variations.changed: the observation becomes the question it usually arrives as in conversation

variations.display: mama deśe janāḥ evam na vadanti.
variations.script: मम देशे जनाः एवम् न वदन्ति।
variations.cue: In my part of the country people do not say it this way.
variations.changed: negated, so the speaker sets his own region apart from what was just claimed

mistake.why: janāḥ is plural and vadati is singular. The plural is vadanti, and its -nti is the only thing in the line that says more than one person is speaking — the noun's -āḥ is easy to lose in the middle of a sentence and the verb ending is not.

sentences.usage: The module's whole claim in one line: the region changes how a word is said, not which word is used. There is no regional grammar here to learn and no home vernacular to be an outsider in.

sentences.display: jñānam iti vadanti, kintu uccāraṇam deśe deśe bhinnam asti.
sentences.script: ज्ञानम् इति वदन्ति, किन्तु उच्चारणम् देशे देशे भिन्नम् अस्ति।
sentences.cue: They say jnanam — but the pronunciation differs from region to region.
sentences.literal: 'knowledge' thus they-say, but pronunciation in-region in-region different is

words.note: Knowledge, a neuter noun. It shares its root with L2-M8's jānāti, 'knows', but neither is a shape of the other and the two are separate rows on this course.
L3-M5's quotative, closing a quoted WORD here rather than a quoted sentence. It always follows what it quotes.
L5-M1's plural of vadati. A region speaks in the plural, so this is the ordinary verb of the module.
L1-M10's 'but', opening its own half. Every sentence in this module that grants something and then turns uses it.

words.cue: pronunciation · the saying of a word
words.note: The pronunciation, cued for the word and not for the case: uccāraṇam names it and uccāraṇe is the 'in' shape. It is what this whole module is about.
The region's 'in' shape again, written twice. Sanskrit distributes by repeating a word, so deśe deśe is 'region after region'.
L4-M5's 'different', neuter here because uccāraṇam is neuter. The ending is copied from the noun, never chosen for the meaning.
L1-M3's copula, written out because the sentence contrasts two halves and a dropped verb would blur them.

sentences.trap: deśe deśe is one word said twice, and it means 'in region after region'. Sanskrit distributes by repeating where English reaches for 'from … to …'.
sentences.sound: GYAA-nam i-ti VA-dan-ti, KIN-tu uch-CHAA-ra-nam DAY-shay DAY-shay BHIN-nam AS-ti. The cluster written jñ is the one this sentence is about: across the north it is said close to 'gy', in Maharashtra close to 'dny', and in the south nearer the two letters it is spelled with. This course says it the pan-Indian way. The double c of uccāraṇam is held — 'uch-chaa', not 'u-chaa'.

variations.display: jñānam iti vadanti, kintu uccāraṇam ekam na asti.
variations.script: ज्ञानम् इति वदन्ति, किन्तु उच्चारणम् एकम् न अस्ति।
variations.cue: They say jnanam — but there is not one pronunciation of it.
variations.changed: the difference is stated as a plain negation instead of being distributed over regions

variations.display: kim uccāraṇam deśe deśe bhinnam asti?
variations.script: किम् उच्चारणम् देशे देशे भिन्नम् अस्ति?
variations.cue: Does the pronunciation differ from region to region?
variations.changed: the observation asked rather than asserted, which is how a learner first raises it

variations.display: jñānam iti vadanti, kintu tatra anyathā vadanti.
variations.script: ज्ञानम् इति वदन्ति, किन्तु तत्र अन्यथा वदन्ति।
variations.cue: They say jnanam — but there they say it differently.
variations.changed: the second half drops the noun and makes the same point with the module's two adverbs

mistake.display: jñānam iti vadanti, kintu uccāraṇam deśe deśe bhinnaḥ asti.
mistake.why: uccāraṇam is NEUTER, so the adjective beside it is bhinnam and not bhinnaḥ. bhinnaḥ is the masculine shape and would need a masculine noun like bhedaḥ or mārgaḥ in front of it.

sentences.usage: The clean way to make the whole observation: name the word, then say that only its saying moves. Neither half accuses anybody of being wrong.

sentences.display: bhedaḥ kevalam uccāraṇe asti, bhāṣā ekā eva.
sentences.script: भेदः केवलम् उच्चारणे अस्ति, भाषा एका एव।
sentences.cue: The difference is only in the pronunciation; the language is one and the same.
sentences.literal: difference only in-pronunciation is, language one indeed

words.note: The difference, a masculine noun and the subject here. It names a gap between two things and says nothing about which of them is right.
L5-M2's 'only', standing in front of what it shrinks. Without it the sentence merely reports a difference; with it, the difference is cut down to size.
uccāraṇam in its 'in' shape. The difference is located inside the saying, which is the claim the whole module rests on.
L1-M3's copula, written out because the sentence contrasts two halves and a dropped verb would blur them.
Language, a feminine noun — so the numeral beside it is ekā and not ekam. It is the language as a thing spoken, which is why this module needs it and L1 did not.
L1-M8's 'one' in its feminine shape, because bhāṣā is feminine. The ending is copied from the noun: ekaḥ, ekā, ekam.
L5-M1's emphasiser, standing after the word it lifts. bhāṣā ekā eva is 'the language is one and NOTHING but one'.

sentences.trap: ekā, not ekam: bhāṣā is feminine and the numeral copies its ending. saṃskṛtam takes ekam and bhāṣā takes ekā, and the word for 'one' never chooses for itself.
sentences.sound: BHAY-dah KAY-va-lam uch-CHAA-ra-nay AS-ti, BHAA-shaa AY-kaa AY-va. The visarga at the end of bhedaḥ is a breathy echo of the vowel in front of it — a light 'h' coloured by that e — which is the same thing it does after the a of rāmaḥ and the a of mārgaḥ. The ṣ of bhāṣā is the retroflex one, said with the tongue curled back.

variations.display: bhedaḥ kevalam uccāraṇe asti, saṃskṛtam ekam eva.
variations.script: भेदः केवलम् उच्चारणे अस्ति, संस्कृतम् एकम् एव।
variations.cue: The difference is only in the pronunciation; Sanskrit is one and the same.
variations.changed: the neuter saṃskṛtam replaces the feminine bhāṣā, and the numeral forks with it

variations.display: kim bhedaḥ kevalam uccāraṇe asti?
variations.script: किम् भेदः केवलम् उच्चारणे अस्ति?
variations.cue: Is the difference only in the pronunciation?
variations.changed: asked rather than asserted — the question a learner puts to a teacher

variations.display: bhedaḥ uccāraṇe asti, kintu bhāṣā ekā eva.
variations.script: भेदः उच्चारणे अस्ति, किन्तु भाषा एका एव।
variations.cue: There is a difference in the pronunciation, but the language is one and the same.
variations.changed: kevalam drops out and kintu carries the contrast instead; the claim is weaker without it

mistake.display: bhedaḥ kevalam uccāraṇe asti, bhāṣā ekam eva.
mistake.why: bhāṣā is feminine, so 'one' beside it is ekā. ekam is the neuter shape and belongs beside saṃskṛtam or uccāraṇam — the numeral copies the noun's ending and never the sense.

sentences.usage: The reassurance a learner needs early and is rarely given: the traditions differ in the mouth and not in the grammar, so nothing said in one of them is wrong in another.
sentences.mnemonic: The difference lives in the mouth.

sentences.display: bhavān kṛṣṇaḥ iti vadati, aham anyathā vadāmi.
sentences.script: भवान् कृष्णः इति वदति, अहम् अन्यथा वदामि।
sentences.cue: You say krishnah; I say it differently.
sentences.literal: you-polite 'black' thus says, I otherwise I-say

words.note: L1-M2's polite 'you', with a THIRD-person verb behind it as it has had for fifty rungs. Nothing in this module changes that.
L2-M3's colour, quoted here as a WORD rather than used as one. It is on the ladder already, which is why the vocalic r in it costs this module nothing.
The quotative closing a single quoted word. Without it the sentence would say that you ARE black rather than that you SAY the word.
L2-M7's 'says', third person because bhavān takes a third-person verb. The pronoun and the ending have to agree even though the meaning is 'you'.
L1-M1's 'I', written out because the sentence sets two speakers against each other and the contrast needs both of them on the page.
'Differently' again, and here it is about one vowel inside one word — which is as small as this module's differences ever get.
L2-M7's first person. Against vadati beside bhavān it is the whole of the contrast: two endings, two speakers, one word being said.

sentences.trap: The word is the same word in both halves of the line. What forks is the vowel written ṛ inside it, and there is no second spelling of kṛṣṇaḥ anywhere in this course.
sentences.sound: bha-VAAN KRISH-nah i-ti VA-da-ti, a-HAM an-ya-THAA va-DAA-mi. The vowel written ṛ (U+1E5B) is the one that moves: across most of the north and east it is said with an i-glide, near 'kri', and in parts of the south and west with a u-glide, nearer 'kru'. Four words already on this ladder carry it — kṛṣṇaḥ, vṛddhaḥ, pṛcchati and pṛṣṭhataḥ — and this course says all four the same way.

variations.display: bhavatī kṛṣṇaḥ iti vadati, aham anyathā vadāmi.
variations.script: भवती कृष्णः इति वदति, अहम् अन्यथा वदामि।
variations.cue: You say krishnah; I say it differently.
variations.changed: the listener is a woman, so the honorific forks and the third-person verb beside it does not

variations.display: bhavān kṛṣṇaḥ iti vadati, aham api tathā vadāmi.
variations.script: भवान् कृष्णः इति वदति, अहम् अपि तथा वदामि।
variations.cue: You say krishnah, and I say it the same way too.
variations.changed: agreement instead of contrast: L3-M3's tathā answers evam the way anyathā refuses it

variations.display: kim bhavān anyathā vadati?
variations.script: किम् भवान् अन्यथा वदति?
variations.cue: Do you say it differently?
variations.changed: the contrast reduced to the question a speaker actually asks, with the quoted word understood

mistake.display: bhavān kṛṣṇaḥ iti vadāmi, aham anyathā vadati.
mistake.why: The two verbs have swapped. bhavān takes the third-person vadati and aham takes the first-person vadāmi; the ENDING carries the person here, and the pronoun in front of it is only confirming what the ending already said.

sentences.usage: The polite way to put a difference of pronunciation: state both halves and claim neither. A learner who announces that their own tradition is the right one has made a claim no teacher makes.
sentences.mnemonic: You say it, I say it, both are said.

sentences.display: śāstram dīrgham asti, kintu sambhāṣaṇam hrasvam asti.
sentences.script: शास्त्रम् दीर्घम् अस्ति, किन्तु सम्भाषणम् ह्रस्वम् अस्ति।
sentences.cue: A treatise runs long, but conversation is short.
sentences.literal: treatise long is, but conversation short is

words.note: A treatise, and by extension the register such a text is written and recited in. śāstram names it, śāstre is the 'in' shape.
L2-M2's 'long', neuter here because śāstram is neuter. It is the grammarians' own word for a long vowel and it measures a whole register the same way.
L1-M3's copula, written out because the sentence contrasts two halves and a dropped verb would blur them.
L1-M10's 'but', opening its own half. Every sentence in this module that grants something and then turns uses it.
Conversation — the spoken register, and the name of what this whole course teaches. sambhāṣaṇam names it, sambhāṣaṇe is the 'in' shape.
L2-M3's 'short', neuter beside sambhāṣaṇam. It is the grammarians' word for a short vowel, and here it is the length of a spoken line.

sentences.trap: dīrgham and hrasvam are the grammarians' own words for a long and a short vowel, and here they measure a whole register. Neither is about a person's height.
sentences.sound: SHAA-stram DEER-gham AS-ti, KIN-tu sam-BHAA-sha-nam HRA-svam AS-ti. The ś of śāstram is the palatal sibilant and the ṣ of sambhāṣaṇam the retroflex one, said with the tongue curled back — two different letters that an English ear hears as one 'sh'. Said at speed the m of śāstram takes the colour of the d after it and comes out close to an n.

variations.display: śāstram dīrgham, sambhāṣaṇam hrasvam.
variations.script: शास्त्रम् दीर्घम्, सम्भाषणम् ह्रस्वम्।
variations.cue: A treatise, long; conversation, short.
variations.changed: both copulas dropped under L1-M3's rule, and the line reads as the maxim it nearly is

variations.display: kim śāstram dīrgham asti?
variations.script: किम् शास्त्रम् दीर्घम् अस्ति?
variations.cue: Does a treatise run long?
variations.changed: one half asked on its own, which is the shape the question comes in

variations.display: sambhāṣaṇam hrasvam asti, kintu śāstram dīrgham asti.
variations.script: सम्भाषणम् ह्रस्वम् अस्ति, किन्तु शास्त्रम् दीर्घम् अस्ति।
variations.cue: Conversation is short, but a treatise runs long.
variations.changed: the halves swap, so the spoken register is the one taken for granted and the written one is the news

mistake.display: śāstram dīrghaḥ asti, kintu sambhāṣaṇam hrasvaḥ asti.
mistake.why: Both nouns are NEUTER, so both adjectives end -am. dīrghaḥ and hrasvaḥ are the masculine shapes and belong beside a word like mārgaḥ — and again the ending is copied from the noun rather than chosen.

sentences.usage: The second axis of the module, and the one a learner meets first in a classroom: śāstram is the register of the recited and the expository, sambhāṣaṇam is the spoken one, and everything on this course is sambhāṣaṇam.
sentences.mnemonic: Long on the page, short in the mouth.

sentences.display: sambhāṣaṇe janāḥ evam vadanti, śāstre anyathā vadanti.
sentences.script: सम्भाषणे जनाः एवम् वदन्ति, शास्त्रे अन्यथा वदन्ति।
sentences.cue: In conversation people say it this way; in a treatise, differently.
sentences.literal: in-conversation people thus say, in-treatise otherwise say

words.note: sambhāṣaṇam in its 'in' shape. The register behaves like a place here, which is exactly the point of pairing this sentence with S01.
L3-M9's janaḥ in its plural. It is people in general here — the speakers of a region, never a named person.
'This way' again, and it points at the spoken register rather than at a region. One adverb, two axes.
L5-M1's plural of vadati. A region speaks in the plural, so this is the ordinary verb of the module.
śāstram in its 'in' shape. The recited and expository register, standing where a region stood in S01.
'Differently', and what differs is sandhi, compound length and pace — never the word itself.

sentences.trap: This is S01's frame with the register standing where the region stood. Both axes take the same sentence, which is why the module can teach the two of them at once.
sentences.sound: sam-BHAA-sha-nay JA-naah AY-vam VA-dan-ti, SHAA-stray an-ya-THAA VA-dan-ti. The locative ending is a plain long e on both nouns. Said at speed janāḥ evam runs on as janā evam, the visarga dropping away in front of the vowel — which is itself one of the things the recited register does more of.

variations.display: sambhāṣaṇe janāḥ evam vadanti, śāstre anyathā.
variations.script: सम्भाषणे जनाः एवम् वदन्ति, शास्त्रे अन्यथा।
variations.cue: In conversation people say it this way; in a treatise, otherwise.
variations.changed: the second verb is dropped and understood, which is what a speaker actually does

variations.display: sambhāṣaṇe aham evam vadāmi, śāstre anyathā vadanti.
variations.script: सम्भाषणे अहम् एवम् वदामि, शास्त्रे अन्यथा वदन्ति।
variations.cue: In conversation I say it this way; in a treatise they say it differently.
variations.changed: the near half goes first person and the far half stays impersonal

variations.display: kim śāstre anyathā vadanti?
variations.script: किम् शास्त्रे अन्यथा वदन्ति?
variations.cue: Do they say it differently in a treatise?
variations.changed: the far half asked alone, which is the question a learner asks after reading one

mistake.display: sambhāṣaṇam janāḥ evam vadanti, śāstram anyathā vadanti.
mistake.why: Both nouns need the 'in' shape. sambhāṣaṇam and śāstram are the naming shapes, and with vadanti behind them they would make the conversation the thing SPOKEN rather than the place of the speaking. The locative sambhāṣaṇe and śāstre is what puts the saying inside them.

sentences.usage: What actually differs between the two registers is sandhi, compound length and pace: the recited line joins everything and runs slower. None of that changes a word, which is why this module writes no second spelling of anything.

sentences.display: saṃskṛtam ekam asti, kintu paramparā ekā na asti.
sentences.script: संस्कृतम् एकम् अस्ति, किन्तु परम्परा एका न अस्ति।
sentences.cue: Sanskrit is one language, but there is not one tradition.
sentences.literal: Sanskrit one is, but tradition one not is

words.note: L1-M1's name for the language, neuter — so the numeral beside it is ekam. The ṛ in it is the vowel S04 is about.
L1-M8's 'one' in its neuter shape, copied from saṃskṛtam. Six words later the same numeral comes out ekā, and the noun is the reason.
L1-M3's copula, written out because the sentence contrasts two halves and a dropped verb would blur them.
L1-M10's 'but', opening its own half. Every sentence in this module that grants something and then turns uses it.
The tradition — a line handed down from teacher to student, feminine. It is what a region has one of and the language does not.
The same numeral in its feminine shape beside paramparā. Two shapes of one word in one sentence, and neither was chosen: both were copied.
L1-M2's negation, standing in front of the verb it denies. na asti is the whole of 'there is not'.

sentences.trap: ekam beside saṃskṛtam and ekā beside paramparā: one word for 'one', with its ending copied from the noun each time. The sentence would be wrong twice over if either shape were used for both.
sentences.sound: SANS-kri-tam AY-kam AS-ti, KIN-tu pa-ram-pa-RAA AY-kaa na AS-ti. The ṛ of saṃskṛtam is the vowel S04 describes and this course says it 'kri' throughout. Said at speed na asti runs together as nāsti, the two a-sounds fusing into one long one.

variations.display: saṃskṛtam ekam, kintu paramparā ekā na asti.
variations.script: संस्कृतम् एकम्, किन्तु परम्परा एका न अस्ति।
variations.cue: Sanskrit is one language, but there is not one tradition.
variations.changed: the first copula drops under L1-M3's rule and the second stays, because a negation needs its verb

variations.display: kim paramparā ekā asti?
variations.script: किम् परम्परा एका अस्ति?
variations.cue: Is there one tradition?
variations.changed: the claim put back as the question it is an answer to

variations.display: bhāṣā ekā asti, kintu paramparā ekā na asti.
variations.script: भाषा एका अस्ति, किन्तु परम्परा एका न अस्ति।
variations.cue: The language is one, but there is not one tradition.
variations.changed: bhāṣā replaces saṃskṛtam, so both halves are feminine and the numeral stops forking

mistake.display: saṃskṛtam ekaḥ asti, kintu paramparā ekaḥ na asti.
mistake.why: ekaḥ is the masculine shape and neither noun is masculine. saṃskṛtam is neuter and takes ekam; paramparā is feminine and takes ekā. One numeral, three endings, and the noun decides every time.

sentences.usage: The module's honest headline. The language is a single thing with a single grammar; the traditions of saying it are many, and not one of them is the language.

sentences.display: bhavān evam vadatu, tatra api janaḥ śṛṇoti.
sentences.script: भवान् एवम् वदतु, तत्र अपि जनः शृणोति।
sentences.cue: Say it this way — a person will hear you there too.
sentences.literal: you-polite thus let-say, there also person hears

words.note: The polite 'you' again. The verb behind it is the third-person request shape, which is how this course has asked for anything since L1-M2.
'This way' — and the way meant is the one the course teaches, not a second one it has kept back.
L2-M7's vadati in the request shape. It is advice rather than an order, and with bhavān in front of it the request is polite.
L1-M7's 'there', standing for any region the speaker is not in. It takes no ending and never will.
L1-M10's 'also', standing AFTER the word it lifts. tatra api is 'there too'; api tatra lifts nothing.
L3-M9's 'person', singular here — one listener rather than a region's worth of speakers, which is the scale a reassurance works at.
L2-M7's 'hears'. It is hearing rather than understanding, and that is the honest claim: the tradition is heard everywhere it is spoken.

sentences.trap: tatra api is 'there too', with api standing after the word it lifts. In front of tatra it would lift nothing at all, which is L1-M10's rule about this course's most misplaced word.
sentences.sound: bha-VAAN AY-vam VA-da-tu, TA-tra a-pi JA-nah SHRI-no-ti. The ṇ of śṛṇoti is the retroflex n, said with the tongue curled back, and the ṛ in front of it is the vowel of S04. Said at speed tatra api runs on as tatrāpi, the two a-sounds fusing into one long one.

variations.display: bhavatī evam vadatu, tatra api janaḥ śṛṇoti.
variations.script: भवती एवम् वदतु, तत्र अपि जनः शृणोति।
variations.cue: Say it this way — a person will hear you there too.
variations.changed: the same advice to a woman; only the honorific forks, because the verb was never second person

variations.display: bhavān evam vadatu, atra api tatra api janaḥ śṛṇoti.
variations.script: भवान् एवम् वदतु, अत्र अपि तत्र अपि जनः शृणोति।
variations.cue: Say it this way — a person hears it here and there alike.
variations.changed: both places named, which is the passport claim stated in full rather than half

variations.display: kim tatra api janaḥ śṛṇoti?
variations.script: किम् तत्र अपि जनः शृणोति?
variations.cue: Will a person hear it there too?
variations.changed: the reassurance asked for instead of offered, which is how a learner usually raises it

mistake.display: bhavān evam vadatu, api tatra janaḥ śṛṇoti.
mistake.why: api stands after the word it lifts and never before it. In front of tatra it lifts nothing, and the sentence loses the 'too' that was its whole point — the same error L1-M10 built a rule around.

sentences.usage: The honest line, and it is worth saying plainly: the tradition this course teaches is a passport and not a disguise. It is understood by teachers and in sambhasana classes everywhere, and it makes nobody a local, because there is no local to be.

sentences.display: mama uccāraṇam bhinnam asti, tathāpi mahyam bhayam na asti.
sentences.script: मम उच्चारणम् भिन्नम् अस्ति, तथापि मह्यम् भयम् न अस्ति।
sentences.cue: My pronunciation is different — even so, I am not afraid of it.
sentences.literal: of-me pronunciation different is, even-so to-me fear not is

words.note: L1-M1's 'of me'. Here it owns the place rather than the speaking, so mama with the 'in' shape behind it is 'in my region'.

words.cue: pronunciation · the saying of a word
words.note: The pronunciation again, and here it belongs to the speaker. mama uccāraṇam is 'my way of saying it' and not 'the way I am supposed to say it'.
'Different', neuter beside uccāraṇam. It says a gap exists and says nothing at all about which side of it is right.
L1-M3's copula, written out because the sentence contrasts two halves and a dropped verb would blur them.
L1-M10's 'even so', opening its half. It grants the fact in front of it and then denies the consequence a learner expected from it.
L1-M1's 'to me'. The fear belongs to somebody in this shape, which is L3-M6's frame and the only way this course says 'I am afraid'.
L3-M6's 'fear', a neuter noun and the SUBJECT of the second half. There is no verb of fearing in this course and none is needed.
The negation in front of its verb. mahyam bhayam na asti is the whole of 'I am not afraid'.

sentences.trap: mahyam bhayam na asti is L3-M6's frame and there is no verb of fearing in it. The fear is a noun that BELONGS to somebody, which is why the speaker stands in the 'to me' shape and not the 'I' shape.
sentences.sound: MA-ma uch-CHAA-ra-nam BHIN-nam AS-ti, ta-THAA-pi MAH-yam BHA-yam na AS-ti. The double c of uccāraṇam is held — 'uch-chaa' and not 'u-chaa' — and the ṇ after it is the retroflex n. Said at speed na asti runs together as nāsti.

variations.display: mama uccāraṇam bhinnam asti, tathāpi mahyam sukham asti.
variations.script: मम उच्चारणम् भिन्नम् अस्ति, तथापि मह्यम् सुखम् अस्ति।
variations.cue: My pronunciation is different — even so, I am content.
variations.changed: the second half turns positive: not the absence of fear but the presence of ease

variations.display: kim bhavataḥ uccāraṇam bhinnam asti?
variations.script: किम् भवतः उच्चारणम् भिन्नम् अस्ति?
variations.cue: Is your pronunciation different?
variations.changed: asked of the listener, which is the way the subject actually comes up between two speakers

variations.display: mama uccāraṇam bhinnam asti, kintu bhāṣā ekā eva.
variations.script: मम उच्चारणम् भिन्नम् अस्ति, किन्तु भाषा एका एव।
variations.cue: My pronunciation is different, but the language is one and the same.
variations.changed: the reassurance moves off the speaker and onto the language, where it is a fact rather than a feeling

mistake.display: mama uccāraṇam bhinnam asti, tathāpi aham bhayam na asti.
mistake.why: bhayam belongs to somebody in the 'to me' shape, so it is mahyam and never aham. With aham the half has two subjects and reads as 'I, fear, is not' — the same error L3-M6 built its whole module around.

sentences.usage: What marks an outsider, answered honestly: almost nothing does. Sanskrit has no native speakers with a local accent to be measured against, so a difference of tradition is a difference and not a mistake.

sentences.display: vṛddhaḥ janaḥ anyathā vadati, tathāpi bhāṣā ekā eva.
sentences.script: वृद्धः जनः अन्यथा वदति, तथापि भाषा एका एव।
sentences.cue: An older person says it differently — even so, the language is one.
sentences.literal: old person otherwise says, even-so language one indeed

words.note: L2-M2's 'old', said of a person and leaning respectful. Masculine here because janaḥ is masculine, and it is not the word for an old object.
'Person' in the singular. The generational observation is made about one speaker at a time, because a generation is not a thing this course can put a plural on.
'Differently' for the third axis — time rather than place or register. The adverb does not change, which is the module's quiet argument that neither does the language.
'Says', third person and singular, agreeing with janaḥ. Nothing in the line is second person.
'Even so', granting the difference before refusing the conclusion. It is the same hinge the module used in S09.
The language, feminine, and the thing that does not move. Everything else in the sentence has moved.
'One' in its feminine shape, copied from bhāṣā. The whole module ends on this agreement.
The emphasiser after the word it lifts: 'one and NOTHING but one'. It is what turns a statement into a closing line.

sentences.trap: This is the generational half of the module and it is deliberately a SHAPE rather than a list. Slang dates faster than a course can be maintained; the observation that an older speaker says a word differently does not.
sentences.sound: VRID-dhah JA-nah an-ya-THAA VA-da-ti, ta-THAA-pi BHAA-shaa AY-kaa AY-va. The ṛ of vṛddhaḥ is the vowel S04 describes, the second of the four words on this ladder that carry it. Said at speed vṛddhaḥ janaḥ joins as vṛddho janaḥ, the visarga turning to o in front of the voiced j.

variations.display: vṛddhaḥ adhyāpakaḥ anyathā vadati, tathāpi bhāṣā ekā eva.
variations.script: वृद्धः अध्यापकः अन्यथा वदति, तथापि भाषा एका एव।
variations.cue: An older teacher says it differently — even so, the language is one.
variations.changed: the speaker is named rather than left general, and the adjective agrees with the new noun unchanged

variations.display: vṛddhaḥ janaḥ anyathā vadati, kintu aham evam vadāmi.
variations.script: वृद्धः जनः अन्यथा वदति, किन्तु अहम् एवम् वदामि।
variations.cue: An older person says it differently, but I say it this way.
variations.changed: the two generations put side by side in one line, with the module's two adverbs doing the work

variations.display: kim vṛddhaḥ janaḥ anyathā vadati?
variations.script: किम् वृद्धः जनः अन्यथा वदति?
variations.cue: Does an older person say it differently?
variations.changed: the observation asked rather than reported, which is the honest shape for a claim about other people

mistake.display: vṛddham janaḥ anyathā vadati, tathāpi bhāṣā ekā eva.
mistake.why: janaḥ is masculine, so 'old' beside it is vṛddhaḥ. vṛddham is the neuter shape and there is no neuter noun in the first half at all — and vṛddhaḥ is the word said of a PERSON, which is the reading this sentence needs.

sentences.usage: The generational observation, and the module stops there on purpose. What an older speaker changes is the saying and often the pace; no list of current words is written, because such a list would be out of date before the course was.

comprehensionPool.cue: Here people say it this way.
In my part of the country the pronunciation is different.
The difference is only in the pronunciation.

comprehensionPool.display: saṃskṛtam ekam asti, kintu uccāraṇam bhinnam asti.
comprehensionPool.script: संस्कृतम् एकम् अस्ति, किन्तु उच्चारणम् भिन्नम् अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: Sanskrit is one, but the pronunciation is different.
In conversation I say it this way.
An older person says it differently.
My teacher says it this way.

comprehensionPool.display: paramparā ekā na asti, kintu bhāṣā ekā eva.
comprehensionPool.script: परम्परा एका न अस्ति, किन्तु भाषा एका एव।
comprehensionPool.cue: There is not one tradition, but the language is one and the same.
Say it this way — I am listening.
